what: The Baldwin Insurance Group (formerly BRP Group) is an insurance broker that sells personal, business and health insurance policies, mostly to US households and mid-sized companies. It also runs a managing general agent that designs and underwrites specialty products such as home insurance for new-build homes.
customers: Homeowners, businesses, and employers buying health benefits, through its own advisors and partnerships with homebuilders and lenders.
money: Commercial and benefits brokerage for mid-sized businesses.
Its managing general agent for specialty home and auto products.
moat: Partnerships with homebuilders and mortgage lenders give it a stream of new customers at the moment they buy a home. Brokerage has high recurring revenue because policies renew.
risks: It has lost money every year shown, mainly from acquisition-related charges and interest costs.
Goodwill of $2.65B, the result of buying many smaller brokers.
Insurance pricing is softening in some lines, which slows commission growth.
opportunities: Revenue grew from $567M in 2021 to $1.85B over the last twelve months.
The forward P/E of about 13 on adjusted earnings is low for a broker.
Large brokers trade at much higher multiples, so a successful turnaround could close the gap.
watch: Organic revenue growth and debt reduction.
view: Baldwin has grown into a large broker by acquisition, but GAAP profits have never followed: it has lost money every year shown, because of amortisation, earnout payments and interest. The forward P/E of 13 on adjusted earnings shows that analysts see underlying profit, and on that basis the shares are cheap compared with larger brokers.

The question is whether the adjustments are legitimate. Some of them, such as amortisation of acquired customer lists, are fair to add back; others, such as repeated earnout charges, look like real costs of the model.

This turns on organic growth and cash flow. If it grows organically and pays down debt, the gap to peers should narrow. If not, the leverage becomes a problem. Analysts rate it a hold, and I agree: it is fairly priced until cash flow proves the adjusted earnings.
bull: Organic growth stays strong, debt falls and the discount to larger brokers narrows.
bear: Softer insurance pricing slows growth and leverage weighs on the shares.
